Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

vignette:
Marcus was twenty-nine years old when he was mugged outside a gas station off the I-95 in Jacksonville, a few blocks from the Coast Guard station where he worked as a boat engineer. It was just after midnight, and he had stopped for coffee on his way back from a late training drill. He never saw the man until the arm locked around his throat from behind. What Marcus remembered most vividly was the pressure-the way his carotid artery felt like a cord being pulled taut-and the sound of his own boots scraping against the asphalt as he was dragged behind a dumpster. The man demanded his wallet, then his watch. Marcus handed them over, but the arm did not loosen. He remembered the smell of stale cigarette smoke and engine grease on the man's sleeve, and the way the stars above the dumpster blurred as his vision started to tunnel. When the man finally let go and ran, Marcus stayed on the ground for what felt like a long time, his hands pressed to his throat, waiting for his breath to come back.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus found that he could not tell the story. When his girlfriend, Elena, asked what had happened, he opened his mouth and nothing came out that felt true. He could describe the sequence-gas station, arm, wallet, release-but the words felt thin and hollow, like describing a movie he had half-watched. The real memory lived in his body: the scrape of concrete against his back, the specific pitch of his own ragged breathing, the way the stars had wobbled and gone gray. He had come to believe that if he could not put it into language, maybe it had not fully happened to him. Sometimes, when he tried to recall the mugging, he felt nothing at all-a strange, hollow numbness, as if he were watching a stranger's life on a screen. The man on the ground was not him; the man on the ground was someone else, someone whose fear Marcus could observe but not feel. That detachment bothered him almost as much as the fear itself.

The memories came in pieces. He would be standing at the engine console on the cutter, checking oil pressure, and suddenly he would feel the asphalt grit against his palms, but he could not remember how he had gotten from the gas station to the ground. There was a gap-a missing splice of time-between the arm around his throat and the stars going blurry. The pieces did not fit together, and every time he tried to force them, his mind skidded sideways like a tire on wet pavement. He started avoiding the night shift. He told his supervisor he preferred day maintenance, and because he was a reliable engineer, no one questioned it. But the avoidance cost him: he stopped volunteering for the late rescue drills that had earned him commendations, and his performance reviews noted that he was "less available for critical operations."

What finally brought Marcus to the clinic was not the memories themselves, but the way they had hollowed out his life. He had stopped driving past the gas station on his way home, taking a twenty-minute detour through residential streets instead. He had stopped walking anywhere after dark, even to take out the trash. Elena had started to notice that he flinched when she came up behind him in the kitchen, and that he had stopped wearing the watch she gave him for his birthday. He did not tell her why. He could not find the words. In the intake, he sat forward in his chair, his hands resting on his knees, and said, quietly, "I need to be able to work nights again. I need to be able to tell my girlfriend what happened. I need to stop feeling like the guy on the ground is someone I don't even know."
